en.sup: Supplied in English. The Greek question has no verb: 'what further need'.

01.r: Opens a condition the writer holds to be untrue.

02.r: Gives weight to the supposition, together with 'then'.
02.n: Abbott-Smith says this particle usually looks ahead to a following δέ and is generally untranslatable. No δέ answers it in this verse; with οὖν it most likely just resumes the argument, which is why most translations leave it out.

03.r: Draws the next step from what has been said about Melchizedek and Levi.
03.n: Abbott-Smith describes the particle as expressing consequence or simple sequence, never standing first in its sentence.

04.r: The full accomplishment of what a priesthood exists to do.
04.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'fulfilment, completion, perfection' and lists only two New Testament uses, this verse and one in Luke. The verse does not say what is brought to completion; it leaves that to the wider argument.

05.r: The priesthood as the means by which perfection would come.

07.r: Belonging to the tribe of Levi.
07.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse as the word's only New Testament use, and notes that in the Septuagint it appears only as the title of Leviticus.

08.r: The institution of priests descended from Levi.
08.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'priesthood' and cites this verse. It differs from ἱερατεία, the 'priestly office' of Hebrews 7:5; this study keeps the two apart.

09.r: The imperfect in a condition contrary to fact: if it were so, which it is not.
09.n: The BSB's 'could have been attained' explains the force of the condition; the Greek has only 'were'.

11.r: Israel, the people who received the law.

12.r: Introduces the aside that explains why the priesthood matters so much.

13.r: The priesthood is the footing on which the law was given.
13.n: Literally 'upon'. Abbott-Smith gives the preposition's primary sense as superposition, 'on, upon'. Most translations read 'under it'; the BSB's 'on this basis' is closer to the preposition.

15.r: The people were given their law in connection with the priesthood.
15.n: A single verb, perfect passive. Abbott-Smith gives the intransitive sense 'to make laws', and for the passive here 'to be furnished with laws'. The perfect marks a giving of law whose result still stands.

17.r: Need beyond what the Levitical priesthood supplied.

18.r: The question implies there would have been no need at all.

19.r: Marks the pattern the new priest follows.

21.r: The pattern or kind of priesthood Melchizedek represents.
21.n: Abbott-Smith's senses run from an arranging, as of troops in battle array, to arrangement, order, and due order. Among its Septuagint uses he lists one in the Psalms, where it renders Hebrew דִּבְרָה.

23.r: A priest of another kind, not one more of the same line.
23.n: Abbott-Smith says this word properly denotes the second of a pair, though in later Greek it encroaches on ἄλλος. Here a different kind of priest fits the contrast with Aaron, a reasonable reading rather than a certainty.

24.r: For a new priest to come on the scene.
24.n: Abbott-Smith records that in the middle voice, as here, the verb is intransitive, to rise. In its causal sense, to raise up, he notes its use of raising from death and of causing someone to appear; here it is simply a new priest arising.

25.r: The new priest the chapter goes on to identify.

26.r: Joins the negative half of the question.

28.r: Marks the pattern he does not follow.

30.r: The priestly line that descends from Aaron.

31.r: Moses' brother, the first high priest of Israel.

32.r: To be described or classed as belonging to Aaron's order.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus reads αὐτῇ, the dative, for αὐτῆς after 'upon', with no difference in English. It also reads the pluperfect νενομοθέτητο, 'had been given the law', for the perfect; the KJV's past tense 'received the law' and the YLT's 'had received law' fit that reading.
